opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think agentic workloads are changing the picture quite a bit. For a while, the mental model for inference was basically a chatbot: a person types a question, the model generates a few hundred tokens, and the person reads it. That shaped the optimizations. We cared a lot about time to first token and about generating tokens faster than a human can read.

With agents, the pattern is different. You have a model that's calling tools, reading files, browsing, writing code, running it, looking at the output, and looping. Often there's no human in the loop for long stretches. So a few things shift.

First, context lengths get much longer. An agent working on a codebase might accumulate hundreds of thousands of tokens of history: tool outputs, file contents, previous attempts. So prefill, attention over long context, and KV cache management become much bigger parts of the cost. That's part of why I've been excited about architectures beyond pure attention, things like state space models and hybrids, where the memory footprint doesn't grow linearly with the context. And on the systems side, things like prefix caching and reusing the KV cache across turns matter a lot, because an agent keeps resending mostly the same context with a little bit appended.

Second, the workload is much more about throughput and total latency for a task than per-token latency for a human reader. If an agent takes fifty steps to finish something, the end-to-end time is what users feel. So decode speed matters even more, because you're generating far more tokens per task, and humans aren't the bottleneck anymore. Techniques like speculative decoding, better batching, and low-precision inference become really important economically.

Third, the traffic is burstier and more heterogeneous. You have long prefills, then short decodes, then a pause while a tool runs, then another prefill. That makes scheduling harder. Do you keep the KV cache in GPU memory while the tool runs? Offload it to CPU memory? Recompute it? Those are the kinds of systems questions that weren't as pressing before.

And finally, I think it pushes us toward co-designing the model and the hardware more tightly. When inference is the dominant cost, and agents can multiply inference demand by ten or a hundred times, every bit of efficiency you get from the architecture, the kernels, and the serving stack compounds. So it's a really exciting time to work on this. The workloads are changing quickly, and there's a lot of room left to optimize.

r001.rationale: It describes agents autonomously calling tools, reading files, browsing, writing and running code, and looping without a human in the loop for long stretches.

r002.rationale: It discusses serving and scheduling around tool execution pauses, including whether to keep, offload, or recompute the KV cache, alongside GPU and inference-speed optimizations.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that agentic workloads change the shape of inference, and that forces us to rethink what we optimize for.

With a chatbot, the pattern is simple: a user types a prompt, the model generates a response, maybe a few hundred tokens, and a human reads it. The bottleneck is per-token latency for one user, and we got pretty good at that. With agents, the model is calling tools, reading the results, planning, backtracking, maybe spawning sub-agents. So you have three things happening at once that weren't true before.

First, the context gets very long. An agent working through a codebase or a multi-step task accumulates tool outputs, file contents, intermediate reasoning, and that can easily be hundreds of thousands of tokens. So the KV cache becomes the dominant cost, not the weights. That's why you're seeing so much work on attention variants with smaller caches, things like multi-head latent attention, grouped query attention pushed further, and hybrid architectures that mix attention with state space or linear layers so that most of the model has constant memory per token. The dense attention layers do the precise retrieval, the SSM layers carry the bulk of the sequence cheaply.

Second, there's a lot of prefix sharing. The agent keeps the same system prompt and the same history, then branches. You might sample multiple candidate actions, or you run the same context through several tool calls. So prefix caching and the ability to fork a KV cache cheaply becomes a first-class systems feature, not an afterthought. Memory management on the GPU starts looking like an operating system problem, paging and sharing, rather than just a kernel problem.

Third, the ratio of prefill to decode shifts around a lot. Tool results come back and you have to ingest a big chunk of text quickly, then decode a bit, then ingest again. So you want prefill to be extremely efficient, which is where things like FlashAttention matter, but you also need the scheduler to interleave prefill and decode across many agents without one starving the other. Disaggregating prefill and decode onto different hardware is one response to that.

And then there's the token volume. An agent might generate ten or a hundred times as many tokens as a human would read for the same task, because most of those tokens are for the model's own benefit. That changes the economics. Throughput per dollar matters more than it did, and it pushes you toward lower precision, FP8 and now FP4 on Blackwell, speculative decoding, and anything that lets you overlap compute and communication across GPUs. The flip side is that latency still matters, because the agent's steps are sequential, so if each step takes a second you have a slow agent. You can't just optimize for batch throughput and call it done.

So I think the optimization target moves from "make one token fast" to "make a long, branching, tool-interleaved trajectory cheap and fast end to end." That's a mix of architecture choices, kernel work, and serving system design, and the three have to be co-designed. The models that win in agentic settings are going to be the ones that were designed with the inference system in mind from the start.

r001.rationale: It contrasts chatbot interactions with agents that call tools, read results, plan, and backtrack, describing a move beyond conversational use.

r002.rationale: It discusses tool-interleaved workflows and optimizations such as prefix caching, scheduling, and prefill/decode handling, extending beyond GPU execution speed alone.

astra-6.text:
I think the big change is that an application might make many model calls to complete one task. The model takes a step, calls a tool, looks at the result, and decides what to do next. So you have to think about the latency and cost of that whole loop.

That changes what you want to optimize. Some steps might benefit from a smaller, faster model; others need more reasoning. And as the agent accumulates tool outputs and conversation history, managing that context becomes important. Can you reuse the computation for the context you’ve already processed? How much memory does that take, and how does it affect the number of requests you can serve?

There’s also a distinction between parallel and sequential work. If you can try several approaches independently, you can use more compute in parallel. But if each step depends on the previous one, latency really matters. So I think the interesting optimization problem is increasingly across the whole application: how do you get a task completed reliably, within a reasonable time and compute budget?

r001.rationale: The response describes a model taking a step, calling a tool, examining the result, and deciding what to do next, identifying autonomous action as a change in application behavior.

r002.rationale: It discusses tool calls and optimizing latency and cost across the application loop, but does not clearly explain optimizing how models connect to human-used tools beyond model execution speed on GPUs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big change is that an application is no longer just one request to a model and one response. You have a model calling tools, looking at the results, deciding what to do next, and potentially launching several other model calls. So the workload becomes much more dynamic.

That changes what you want to optimize. For a single model call, you might focus on tokens per second. For an agent, you care about how long it takes to finish the task and how much that task costs. If there are ten sequential steps, latency at each step really matters. If there are independent branches, you want to run those in parallel.

There are also opportunities around reusing context. Different calls might share a long prefix, so you don’t want to recompute that every time. But keeping all that state around puts pressure on memory, and now scheduling and managing the KV cache become important.

So I think the interesting optimization problem expands beyond making an individual kernel faster. You still need that, but you also need to understand the whole application: which calls are on the critical path, what work you can reuse, and where you can use a smaller model without hurting the final result.

r001.rationale: It describes models calling tools, evaluating results, choosing next steps, and launching further calls, explicitly contrasting this with a single request and response.

r002.rationale: It says optimization must cover the whole application beyond kernel speed, but does not clearly identify optimizing how models connect to human-used tools as a requirement.
